newsitem.title: KENYA: Sierra Leone faces severe food shortages, FAO says.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone faces severe food shortages, FAO says.

text.p: The U.N. Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO) warned on Thursday famine could develop in Sierra Leone if insecurity was allowed to persist.

FAO said in a report that most international aid workers had been evacuated from Sierra Leone and rehabilitation projects as well as the repatriation of 318,000 refugees from neighbouring countries had been suspended.
"The food situation has tightened in main towns, with the price of rice tripling in (the capital) Freetown," FAO said.

"Humanitarian agencies have started limited food distributions to vulnerable people in Freetown, Bo, Kenema and Makeni, while cross-border operations from Ivory Coast and Guinea allow limited provision of food to affected persons in rural areas," it added.

"Insecurity has severely hampered agricultural activities, especially the planting of the main crops which normally takes place from April to June," said FAO, adding it would hit this year's food production.

"Contrary to previous expectations following the return of peace, planted areas are likely to be sharply reduced as farmers abandon their farms while others are discouraged from cultivating larger areas," FAO added.
The former British colony is being squeezed by an air, land and sea embargo from its West African neighbours, demanding the restoration of an elected government toppled by soldiers on May 25.
Diplomats in New York said on Wednesday the U.N. Security Council might impose a travel and arms ban on Sierra Leone, possibly next week, if its military junta insisted on holding on to power.

FAO said Sierra Leone would continue to rely heavily on food aid to meet its needs. Before the upheaval, cereal import needs were estimated at 260,000 tonnes and the food aid requirement at 80,000 tonnes.
Cereal aid needed to support resettlement and rehabilitation was pegged at 60,500 tonnes. FAO did not give an overall figure for production in Sierra Leone or its total food requirements.
FAO said in contrast the food situation in neighbouring Liberia was improving and production was expected to increase this year after relative peace and stability helped farming.
"Rainfall as of the end of June was normal and the planting period for rain-fed rice had just ended," FAO said.
It said the overall food situation in sub-Saharan Africa was satisfactory, reflecting generally adequate harvests in many parts in 1996 and normal results in southern Africa this year.
FAO said food supply difficulties would persist in Rwanda, Burundi and east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo -- the former Zaire -- where the security situation was still tense.
